newsitem.title: FINLAND: British buyer brings bounce to Finland's Amer.
newsitem.headline: British buyer brings bounce to Finland's Amer.

text.p: A British investor Monday agreed to take over a majority in money-losing Finnish sporting goods group Amer, owner of the key Wilson tennis and golfing brands, ending months of uncertainty over the group's future.

Amer's stock, suspended for most of the session, volleyed to a new year high in the last half hour of trade in initial enthusiasm for the plan by Jonathan Bryan Guinness, the third Lord Moyne, to buy control from Finnish institutional investors.
The stock closed at 107.00 markka ($20.72), up 6.00 markka ($1.16) or nearly 6 percent, after at one stage hitting 116.50 ($22.57).

Guinness, who last month bought control of Swedish investment fund Trustor, pledged to keep Amer's focus on boosting its key brands and said its chief executive, former national skiing champion Roger Talermo, would stay in charge.
"This is not an in-and-out situation," he told Reuters. "Amer could even be at the centre of a very powerful group."

Guinness, who left the board of British brewer Guinness Plc in 1988 when his family's holding shrank too low to justify two board seats, said last month's Swedish buy signalled a return to business after a spell mainly as a writer.
Although both deals were close in time and geography, Guinness said there was no "inherent connection" between them.

Pending formal approval by four holders of vote-heavy K-shares who currently control 90.5 percent of votes in the company, Guinness will buy an eventual 58.4 percent of votes in the group for a total 301 million markka ($58.3 million).

The K-shareholders, a diverse group of Finnish institutions with no industrial or strategic interest in the sports business, have for about a year been looking to sell their controlling holding of the unlisted K stock.
News of the deal with Guinness came on the day shareholders were meeting to approve a plan to convert the K stock into A-series shares, enabling them to be freely traded.

Amer has said it hopes to return to a profit in 1998 after problems mainly in its golfing equipment division knocked it to a 234 million-markka ($45 million) loss in 1996. It expects to stay in the red this year.
